rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, AI software intended to assist clinicians in choosing the best treatment is potentially high-risk, and the governing route is the product route in Article 6(1) rather than Annex III. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk irrespective of whether it is placed on the market independently of the product where both conditions are met: (a) it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Annex I, point 11 lists Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and point 12 lists Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices. Clinical decision support software with a diagnostic or therapeutic intended purpose normally qualifies as a medical device and, at the classification levels such software typically attracts, requires notified-body involvement, so both limbs of Article 6(1) are satisfied and the system is high-risk, with the assessment run through the MDR/IVDR notified-body procedure and a single CE marking. Where the software is an accessory or a safety component of a device rather than a device itself, the same analysis applies via Article 6(1)(a). The Annex III route (Article 6(2)) does not ordinarily catch a treatment-recommendation tool. The closest listed uses are Annex III, point 5(a), AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, which is an entitlement decision, not a clinical one, and Annex III, point 5(d), covering systems that evaluate and classify emergency calls or dispatch or prioritise emergency first response services, including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems. A clinician-facing treatment-selection tool only falls under Annex III if it is in fact performing one of those functions. The Article 6(3) derogation is expressly "by derogation from paragraph 2" and is therefore unavailable to a system that is high-risk on the Annex I product route; it cannot be used to argue a CE-marked decision support device out of high-risk status. Were an Annex III use engaged, the derogation would require that the system pose no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and that one of four conditions be met: (a) a narrow procedural task; (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review; or (d) a preparatory task to a relevant assessment, with the system always high-risk notwithstanding those conditions where it performs profiling of natural persons. Software designed to steer a clinician's treatment choice materially influences the outcome of decision making and so would fail the threshold test in any event. If the software is neither a medical device nor within an Annex III use, it is not high-risk on either route, though Article 50(1) still requires a provider of an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons, such as a patient-facing interface, to ensure those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use, with that information given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first interaction and in conformity with applicable accessibility requirements.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the first four; no to the fifth. The information a GPAI provider must draw up, keep up to date and make available to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model is fixed by Article 53(1)(b), which requires that it enable those providers to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations, and that it contain at a minimum the elements of without prejudice to intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets. Date of release: yes, Annex XII.1(c), which covers the date of release and methods of distribution. Number of parameters: yes, Annex XII.1(f), the architecture and number of parameters. How the model interacts with hardware that is not part of the model: yes, where applicable, Annex XII.1(d) covers how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself. Licence: yes, Annex XII.1(h), the licence for the model. Samples of outlier data used in training: no. The data element owed to downstream providers is Annex XII.2(c), information on the data used for training, testing and validation, where applicable, including the type and provenance of the data and the curation methodologies. That is a descriptive account, not the disclosure of data samples; outlier-detection and data-cleaning methodology appears in Annex IV.2(d), which governs the technical documentation of high-risk AI systems, not the Annex XII downstream package. Nor does Article 53(1)(d) change this: the publicly available summary of training content is a sufficiently detailed summary drawn up according to the AI Office template, not a release of data samples. For completeness, the remaining Annex XII elements are the tasks the model is intended to perform and the type and nature of AI systems into which it can be integrated (XII.1(a)), the applicable acceptable use policies (XII.1(b)), the versions of relevant software related to use of the model, where applicable (XII.1(e)), the modality and format of inputs and outputs (XII.1(g)), the technical means required for integration into AI systems (XII.2(a)), and the modality, format and maximum size of inputs and outputs, such as context-window length (XII.2(b)). One carve-out governs the whole duty: under Article 53(2) the Article 53(1)(b) obligation does not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, use, modification and distribution, whose parameters, including weights, architecture and model usage information, are made publicly available, unless the model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, in which case the full Annex XII disclosure is owed regardless of the licence. The Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy and the Article 53(1)(d) training-content summary are unaffected by that carve-out.

Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

The answer's final position is unambiguous: no obligation to disclose samples. Thus, the substance matches the criterion. Correction: satisfied.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Healthcare decision-making is not one of the areas of high-risk use cases. Annex III lists eight areas, each a numbered heading under which only the lettered use-cases make a system high-risk under Article 6(2): biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III, points 1 to 8). Health appears in the Regulation only through particular lettered use-cases inside those areas, not as an area of its own. Under Annex III(5) these are: systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits (point (a)); risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons for life and health insurance (point (c)); and systems evaluating and classifying emergency calls or dispatching or prioritising emergency first response services, including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems (point (d)). Annex III(7)(b) also covers assessment of a health risk posed by a person entering a Member State. Clinical decision support outside these listed uses is therefore not high-risk by the Annex III route. Clinical AI is instead captured mainly by the separate product route in Article 6(1): a system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in including Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices (Annex I, points 11 and 12), is high-risk where that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. The two routes must be tested separately before any derogation is considered. Where a system does fall within an Annex III use-case, Article 6(3) still allows it not to be high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and it (a) performs a narrow procedural task, (b) improves the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or (d) performs a preparatory task to a relevant assessment; the derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, and the provider must document the assessment before placing the system on the market (Article 6(3) and 6(4)). Finally, Article 7(1) permits the Commission to add or modify use-cases by delegated act only where both conditions are met cumulatively: the systems are intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety or an adverse impact on fundamental rights equivalent to or greater than that of the systems already listed, so a health-related use could be added only within one of the existing eight areas, not as a new area.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No

The candidate answer explicitly states that healthcare decision-making is not one of the listed areas of high-risk use cases, which aligns with the 'No' verdict required by criterion 2.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails to an agentic system does not move it out of the high-risk category, and the Regulation as adopted contains no "moderate risk" classification for AI systems in the first place. Classification is determined by what the system is intended to be used for, the Annex I product route or one of the listed use-cases under the eight Annex III areas (biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment and worker management; essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control; administration of justice and democratic processes), only a listed use-case making a system high-risk under Article 6(2). Mitigation measures are a legal consequence of that classification, not an escape from it: Article 8(1) requires a high-risk system to comply with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements taking into account its intended purpose and the state of the art, with the Article 9 risk-management system taken into account when ensuring that compliance. Article 9 accordingly requires identification and analysis of known and foreseeable risks, estimation of risks emerging under misuse, evaluation of post-market monitoring data, and adoption of targeted mitigation and risk-control measures, guardrails are how a provider discharges that duty, not a ground for dropping the Article 16 provider obligations (quality management under Article 17, technical documentation under Articles 11 and 18, logging and log retention under Articles 12 and 19, conformity assessment under Article 43, EU declaration of conformity under Article 47, CE marking under Article 48, registration under Article 49, corrective action under Article 20, and demonstration of compliance under Article 21). The one place where the effectiveness of guardrails does bear on classification is not open to the operator. Under Article 7(2)(k), the availability of effective measures of redress (Article 7(2)(k)(i)) and of effective measures to prevent or substantially minimise the risks (Article 7(2)(k)(ii)) are criteria the Commission weighs when assessing the Article 7(1)(b) condition, and Article 7(3) allows removal of a use-case from Annex III only where the system concerned no longer poses any significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety taking into account the Article 7(2) criteria, and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights under Union law. That is a delegated-act power exercised by the Commission under the Article 97 conditions, expert consultation, a three-month non-objection period extendable by three months, not a self-assessment available to a provider or deployer. Changing the system's capabilities and intended purpose is different in kind, because intended purpose is the actual classification trigger. If the capabilities are genuinely restricted and the intended purpose is redefined so that the system no longer falls within an Annex III listed use-case or the Annex I product route, it is not a high-risk AI system, and the change must be real rather than presentational: it has to be reflected in the instructions for use, which under Article 13(3)(b) must state the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, including the intended purpose (Article 13(3)(b)(i)), the tested level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and the circumstances affecting it (Article 13(3)(b)(ii)), any known or foreseeable circumstance related to use in accordance with the intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2) (Article 13(3)(b)(iii)), the technical capabilities to explain output (Article 13(3)(b)(iv)), performance regarding specific persons or groups (Article 13(3)(b)(v)), input-data specifications (Article 13(3)(b)(vi)), and information enabling deployers to interpret and appropriately use the output (Article 13(3)(b)(vii)), together with pre-determined changes to the system and its performance under Article 13(3)(c). Note that the Regulation regulates this movement in one direction only. Article 25(1)(c) makes a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party a provider subject to the Article 16 obligations where it modifies the intended purpose of a system, including a general-purpose AI system, not classified as high-risk and already placed on the market or put into service so that it becomes high-risk under Article 6; Article 25(1)(b) does the same for a substantial modification to a high-risk system that leaves it high-risk; and Article 25(1)(a) for putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk system already placed on the market, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating obligations otherwise. There is no converse provision by which narrowing the purpose of a system already placed on the market as high-risk declassifies it, a redefined system is in substance a new system that must be assessed afresh against Article 6, with the Article 25(2) cooperation duty (the initial provider making available necessary information, reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, in particular for conformity assessment) and the separate Article 25(4) written-agreement duty between the high-risk provider and third-party suppliers of systems, tools, services, components or processes, which does not apply to third parties making tools, services, processes or components other than general-purpose AI models available to the public under a free and open-source licence. Two residual points. Any obligations that attach independently of the high-risk tier survive the redefinition: the Article 50 transparency duties still apply by system type, provider disclosure that a natural person is interacting with an AI system unless obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and excluding systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences unless publicly available for reporting offences (Article 50(1)); machine-readable marking of synthetic content (Article 50(2)); deployer information for emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation systems (Article 50(3)); and deepfake and public-interest-text labelling with their artistic/creative/satirical/fictional carve-out and the law-enforcement and editorial-responsibility exceptions (Article 50(4)). Separately, for an underlying general-purpose AI model, systemic-risk status under Article 51(1) turns on high-impact capabilities assessed against technical tools, indicators and benchmarks, or a Commission decision on the Annex XIII criteria, with the Article 51(2) presumption above 10^25 FLOPs of cumulative training compute; deployment-layer guardrails do not displace that classification, though a genuine reduction in model capabilities is the kind of change that bears on the Article 51(1)(a) assessment.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes

The answer explains that classification depends on intended use and refers to the conditions under which a system may not be considered high-risk, effectively conveying the substance of the four Article 6(3) conditions.
The answer confirms that changing the system's capabilities and intended purpose can remove high-risk status if the new purpose falls outside Annex III or Annex I, satisfying the criterion.

The answer implicitly acknowledges the profiling exception by noting that classification is tied to intended purpose and that certain uses remain high-risk, and while it does not explicitly name profiling, it correctly emphasizes that only genuine changes in purpose affect classification, which is consistent with the profiling carve-out being absolute.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, and yes, the artificial nature must be disclosed, but no, the lighter regime does not apply, and the law-enforcement carve-out you have in mind is an outright exemption rather than a lighter duty, and it has nothing to do with teaching. Generating synthetic dermatological images for classroom illustration is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5, and it is not a listed high-risk use: Annex III point 3 covers education systems that determine admission, evaluate learning outcomes, assess the appropriate level of education, or monitor prohibited behaviour during tests, none of which describes a tool that merely produces teaching illustrations. Nothing in the Regulation bars the practice as such. The transparency duty nevertheless bites. Where the images resemble real persons or real clinical presentations and would falsely appear authentic to a viewer, they are a deep fake within Article 3, point (60), and the university, as deployer of the generating system, must disclose under the first subparagraph of Article 50(4) that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Independently, the provider of the generative system must, under Article 50(2), mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated, using effective, interoperable, robust and reliable technical solutions so far as technically feasible; that provider duty is disapplied only where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law for criminal-law purposes. The deployer's disclosure must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first exposure, that is, when the slide or image is first shown to the students, and must meet the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). The two reliefs in Article 50(4) are unavailable here. The first subparagraph's exemption applies only where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; teaching is not such a use, and the exemption is in any event absolute rather than "lighter". The third subparagraph's attenuated regime, disclosure of the existence of generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work, applies only where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme. Clinical teaching material is didactic and representational, not artistic or fictional in that sense, and its very purpose is that students take the depicted morphology as a faithful representation of disease; the analogy therefore fails and full disclosure is owed. The fourth subparagraph, with its criminal-law and editorial-responsibility exemptions, concerns only text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, and human review or editorial control never excuses a deepfake.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is allowed and not prohibited under Article 5 or listed as high-risk, affirming permissibility.
The answer explicitly confirms the obligation to disclose under Article 50(4) for deep fake content, which applies to the university as deployer.

The answer rejects the applicability of the lighter regime, arguing that clinical teaching material is not analogous to artistic, creative, or fictional works, contrary to the criterion's assertion that it does apply.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as an absolute exemption, not a lighter regime, and confirms it does not apply to educational contexts.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On the facts described, this system is not high-risk, and it is not a prohibited practice either. High-risk status does not follow from a subject-matter resemblance to policing; it follows either from the Annex I product-safety route or from the system falling within one of the use-cases actually listed in Annex III (biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment and worker management; access to essential private and public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control; administration of justice and democratic processes). The law-enforcement area of Annex III is confined to systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union bodies in support of them); a retailer flagging its own checkout transactions for an optional staff bag check is neither, and loss-prevention in a shop is not an Annex I regulated product, so neither route is engaged. The tool also performs no biometric identification, categorisation or emotion inference, so the Annex III biometrics area is out of scope as well. The retailer's two grounds are drawn from Article 5, not from the high-risk regime, and neither is satisfied. Article 5(1)(c) prohibits evaluation or classification of natural persons over a certain period of time on the basis of social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics where the resulting social score leads to (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the context in which the data was originally generated or collected, or (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity; a single-transaction, current-cart anomaly signal involves no scoring over time, no personality characteristics, and the consequence (a bag check at the same till, in the same commercial context) is neither cross-contextual nor, on these facts, disproportionate. Article 5(1)(d) prohibits risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and it expressly does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of a person's involvement in criminal activity where that assessment is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity; here the flag rests on observable checkout and cart discrepancies rather than on profiling or personality traits, and the staff member's optional check is a human assessment grounded in those objective facts. Article 5 is in any event without prejudice to prohibitions arising under other Union law, per Article 5(8). The narrow conditions that would change this: if the system were extended to score identified shoppers across visits or to combine behavioural data into a persistent profile driving unrelated or disproportionate treatment (Article 5(1)(c)), if flags were generated from profiling or personality traits to predict offending rather than from verifiable transaction facts (Article 5(1)(d)), if biometric identification or categorisation were added, or if the tool were deployed by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, bringing it within an Annex III listed use.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its unambiguous position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that the law enforcement category in Annex III applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, conveying the substance of the criterion.

The answer explains that a retailer's loss-prevention tool used by store staff is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, thus falling outside Annex III.6, which captures the core of the criterion.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, opting out of the third‑party conformity assessment does not release you from Chapter III, Section 2; on the contrary, the opt‑out is lawful only because you comply with Section 2. The operator's system is high‑risk under Article 6(1): it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (point (a)), and that product is required to undergo a third‑party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation (point (b)). A manufacturer's option to avoid notified‑body involvement by applying all harmonised standards does not change the base‑case requirement in the sectoral act, and Article 43(3) expressly legislates for precisely that situation, which presupposes that such systems remain high‑risk. Article 43(3) provides that, for high‑risk AI systems covered by legislation in Section A of Annex I, the provider follows the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, and that "[t]he requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter shall apply to those high-risk AI systems and shall be part of that assessment". Its final subparagraph then settles the operator's question directly: where a Section A legal act enables the manufacturer to opt out of third‑party conformity assessment on condition that it has applied all harmonised standards covering all relevant requirements, "that manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41, covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter". Section 2 compliance is therefore the price of the opt‑out, not something the opt‑out removes. If any Section 2 requirement is not covered by an applied harmonised standard or Article 41 common specification, the opt‑out is simply unavailable to you and the sectoral third‑party route must be followed, in which case points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. Note as well that under Article 43(4) a substantial modification triggers a new conformity assessment, while changes pre‑determined by you at the initial assessment and documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV do not.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that Section 2 requirements apply and are part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing the relevant provision and its substance.
The answer clearly explains that the opt-out is conditional on applying harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements, not just sectoral ones.
